extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film fans, and researchers interested in stand-up comedy films
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and description of a feature-length stand-up comedy concert film (production, distribution, content, reception, and legacy). Focuses on attributes that make such a film notable or successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success / box office
rubrics_metrics.description: As of December 2024, it is the highest-grossing stand-up comedy concert film ever released, making $50.5 million in the United States and Canada.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gross revenue and records (e.g., surpassing earlier concert films) as measures of commercial impact and relative success; the article also converts to inflation-adjusted figures (noting $143 million in 2025 dollars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical release / distribution scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike Delirious, Raw received a wide theatrical release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution breadth (wide theatrical release versus limited/release-only-at-venues) is a distinguishing production/distribution attribute that affects reach and box-office potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filming venue, runtime, and production credits
rubrics_metrics.description: The 90-minute show was filmed at the Felt Forum, a venue in the Madison Square Garden complex in New York City.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production details (runtime, venue, director, production company) provide context for format and staging — e.g., filmed concert at a major venue, directed by Robert Townsend, produced by Eddie Murphy Productions and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPAA rating and content edits
rubrics_metrics.description: The film was originally given an 'X' rating by the MPAA, but several cuts from Murphy's performance were made to secure an 'R' rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory/rating outcomes and the edits made to achieve them are relevant criteria — they affect the film's audience, distribution options, and public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitness / profanity count
rubrics_metrics.description: The film contained the word "fuck" 223 times, setting the record for highest "fuck count" ever in a feature-length, theatrically released film at the time (surpassing Scarface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures of explicitness (e.g., swear-word counts, taboo subject matter) are used to characterize the film's edginess and shock value; the article notes the record and that it was held until 1990 when Goodfellas surpassed it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception — positive notices
rubrics_metrics.description: The New York Times praised Eddie Murphy's stand-up routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive major-publication reviews and aggregated praise are key indicators of artistic or comedic quality; the article also cites a Rotten Tomatoes consensus praising the film as "a searingly unbridled and viciously funny showcase from one of comedy's best."

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception — negative or mixed notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Michael Wilmington of the Los Angeles Times wrote that it was "a surprisingly poor concert film of Murphy’s stand-up act," saying Murphy is "like a musician with fabulous technique playing 'Chopsticks.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasting critiques that separate performer skill from filmmaking craft (e.g., excellent technique but poor presentation/structure) help evaluate both the live performance and its cinematic translation; include split opinions such as Siskel and Ebert's split-decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural influence and legacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Alfonso Ribeiro said he drew inspiration from Murphy's depiction of white people dancing in developing "The Carlton"; Gabriel Iglesias credits Raw for inspiring him to become a comedian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessing influence on other performers, references in later works, and the film's role in shaping culture or careers is a measure of lasting significance and legacy.
